concepts.topicTitle: Introduction and the era before factories
concepts.label: Images of Progress and the History of Industrialisation
concepts.cardText: Pictures from around 1900 glorified machines and technology: an angel of progress carrying the flag of the new century with railway, camera, machines, printing press and factory floating behind her, and a trade magazine picture of two magicians contrasting Aladdin, who represents the East and the past, with the modern mechanic, who represents the West and modernity. Within this triumphant account the modern world is associated with rapid technological change, machines and factories, railways and steamships, and the history of industrialisation becomes simply a story of development. The chapter asks whether industrialisation always rests on rapid technological development, and looks first at Britain, the first industrial nation, and then at India, where the pattern of industrial change was conditioned by colonial rule.

concepts.topicTitle: Introduction and the era before factories
concepts.label: Proto-Industrialisation
concepts.cardText: We often associate industrialisation only with factories, but even before factories dotted the landscape in England and Europe there was large-scale industrial production for an international market that was not based on factories; historians call this phase proto-industrialisation. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, merchants from towns moved to the countryside, supplying money to peasants and artisans to produce for an international market. They could not expand production in towns because urban crafts and trade guilds were powerful: guilds were associations of producers that trained craftspeople, controlled production, regulated competition and prices, and restricted entry into the trade, and rulers granted them monopoly rights. So merchants turned to the countryside, where open fields were disappearing and commons were being enclosed, so cottagers and poor peasants who depended on commons needed new income and eagerly accepted merchants' advances. Proto-industrial income supplemented their shrinking income from cultivation and allowed fuller use of family labour.

concepts.topicTitle: Introduction and the era before factories
concepts.label: The Proto-Industrial System
concepts.cardText: Within the proto-industrial system a close relationship developed between the town and the countryside: merchants were based in towns but the work was done mostly in the countryside. An English merchant clothier bought wool from a wool stapler and carried it to the spinners; the yarn was taken in later stages to weavers, fullers and dyers, and the finishing was done in London before the export merchant sold the cloth in the international market, so London became known as a finishing centre. The system was part of a network of commercial exchanges controlled by merchants, with goods produced by a vast number of producers within their family farms, not in factories. Each merchant employed 20 to 25 workers at each stage, so each clothier controlled hundreds of workers.

concepts.topicTitle: Introduction and the era before factories
concepts.label: The Coming Up of the Factory
concepts.cardText: The earliest factories in England came up by the 1730s, but only in the late eighteenth century did their number multiply. The first symbol of the new era was cotton: in 1760 Britain imported 2.5 million pounds of raw cotton, and by 1787 this soared to 22 million pounds. A series of eighteenth-century inventions increased the efficacy of each step of production (carding, twisting and spinning, and rolling), enhanced output per worker and made stronger threads possible. Then Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill; the costly new machines could be purchased, set up and maintained in the mill, and all processes were brought together under one roof and management. This allowed more careful supervision, a watch over quality and regulation of labour, which had been difficult when production was in the countryside. Factories became an intimate part of the English landscape, and contemporaries, dazzled by the mills, almost forgot the bylanes and workshops where production still continued.

concepts.topicTitle: Introduction and the era before factories
concepts.label: The Pace of Industrial Change
concepts.cardText: Industrial change in Britain was not as rapid or as complete as the factory image suggests. First, the most dynamic industries were cotton and metals: cotton led the first phase up to the 1840s and then iron and steel, as railways expanded demand; by 1873 Britain exported iron and steel worth about 77 million pounds, double the value of its cotton exports. Second, new industries could not easily displace traditional ones: even at the end of the nineteenth century, less than 20 per cent of the workforce was in technologically advanced sectors, and much textile output came from domestic units. Third, traditional industries such as food processing, building, pottery, glass work, tanning and furniture-making grew through small, ordinary innovations. Fourth, technological change was slow because new technology was expensive, machines often broke down and repairs were costly; James Watt's improved steam engine patented in 1781 found no buyers for years, and at the beginning of the nineteenth century there were no more than 321 steam engines in England. The typical mid-nineteenth-century worker was not a machine operator but a traditional craftsperson and labourer.

concepts.label: Why Industrialists Preferred Hand Labour
concepts.cardText: In Victorian Britain there was no shortage of human labour: poor peasants and vagrants moved to cities in large numbers, and where labour is plentiful, wages are low. So industrialists had no problem of labour shortage or high wage costs and did not want machines that got rid of human labour and needed large capital investment. In many industries, such as gas works, breweries, book-binding and printing, and ship repair, demand for labour was seasonal, so industrialists preferred hand labour employed for the season. A range of products could be produced only by hand: machines were oriented to uniforms and standardised goods for a mass market, but demand was often for intricate designs and specific shapes, such as 500 varieties of hammers and 45 kinds of axes, which needed human skill. The upper classes preferred handmade things, which came to symbolise refinement and class, and machine-made goods were exported to the colonies. In countries with labour shortage, like nineteenth-century America, industrialists were keen on mechanical power.

concepts.label: Life of the Workers
concepts.cardText: The abundance of labour affected the lives of workers. Hundreds tramped to the cities as news of jobs spread, but getting a job depended on networks of friendship and kin; many job-seekers waited weeks, spending nights under bridges or in night shelters. Seasonal work meant prolonged periods without work. Wages increased somewhat in the early nineteenth century but told little about welfare: when prices rose sharply during the Napoleonic War the real value of earnings fell, and income depended also on the number of days of work. About 10 per cent of the urban population were extremely poor till the mid-nineteenth century, and in slumps such as the 1830s unemployment went up to between 35 and 75 per cent in different regions. The fear of unemployment made workers hostile to new technology: women who survived on hand spinning attacked the Spinning Jenny, which by turning one wheel set many spindles in motion and reduced labour demand. After the 1840s building activity in cities opened up greater opportunities, and the number of workers in the transport industry doubled in the 1840s and doubled again in the next 30 years.

concepts.label: The Age of Indian Textiles
concepts.cardText: Before the age of machine industries, silk and cotton goods from India dominated the international market in textiles; coarser cottons were produced in many countries, but the finer varieties often came from India. A vibrant sea trade operated through main pre-colonial ports: Surat connected India to the Gulf and Red Sea ports, and Masulipatam and Hoogly traded with Southeast Asia. Indian merchants and bankers financed production, and supply merchants gave advances to weavers, procured cloth from weaving villages and carried it to the ports. By the 1750s this network controlled by Indian merchants was breaking down as European companies gained concessions and then monopoly rights. The old ports of Surat and Hoogly declined, exports fell dramatically, credit dried up and local bankers went bankrupt; the value of trade through Surat slumped from Rs 16 million in the late seventeenth century to Rs 3 million by the 1740s. While Surat and Hoogly decayed, Bombay and Calcutta grew, with trade controlled by European companies and carried in European ships.

concepts.label: What Happened to Weavers? The Company and the Gomasthas
concepts.cardText: After the consolidation of East India Company power in the 1760s, textile exports did not initially decline because British cotton industries had not yet expanded and Indian fine textiles were in great demand, so the Company was keen to expand them. Before it had political power, the Company found it difficult to secure regular supplies because the French, Dutch, Portuguese and local traders competed, and weavers could bargain. Once it established political power, it asserted a monopoly right to trade and developed a system of management and control to eliminate competition, control costs and ensure regular supplies. First, it tried to eliminate existing traders and brokers and gain direct control over the weaver by appointing a paid servant, the gomastha, to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine quality. Second, it prevented Company weavers from dealing with other buyers through advances: weavers given loans to buy raw material had to hand over the cloth to the gomastha. The gomasthas were outsiders who marched into villages with sepoys and peons and beat and flogged weavers for delays; weavers lost the space to bargain, the price was miserably low and loans tied them to the Company. Weavers deserted villages, revolted, or gave up weaving for agricultural labour.

concepts.label: Manchester Comes to India
concepts.cardText: By the beginning of the nineteenth century a long decline of textile exports from India began: piece-goods accounted for 33 per cent of India's exports in 1811-12 but no more than 3 per cent by 1850-51. As English cotton industries developed, industrial groups pressurised the government to impose import duties so that Manchester goods could sell in Britain without competition, and persuaded the East India Company to sell British manufactures in Indian markets. British cotton goods rose from virtually nothing at the end of the eighteenth century to over 31 per cent of the value of Indian imports by 1850 and over 50 per cent by the 1870s. Indian weavers faced two problems at once: their export market collapsed and the local market shrank, glutted with cheap Manchester imports made by machines at lower costs. By the 1850s reports spoke of decline and desolation. By the 1860s weavers could not get enough good raw cotton: when the American Civil War cut off supplies from the US, Britain turned to India, the price of raw cotton shot up and weavers were forced to buy at exorbitant prices. By the end of the century Indian factories began flooding the market with machine-goods.

concepts.label: The First Factories and the Early Entrepreneurs
concepts.cardText: The first cotton mill in Bombay came up in 1854 and went into production two years later; by 1862 four mills were at work, jute mills came up in Bengal from 1855, the Elgin Mill started in Kanpur in the 1860s, and the first Madras spinning and weaving mill began by 1874. Many business groups had origins in the China trade: the British exported opium to China and took tea to England, and Indians were junior players in this trade, providing finance, procuring supplies and shipping consignments. Dwarkanath Tagore made his fortune in the China trade and set up six joint-stock companies in the 1830s and 1840s; Parsis like Dinshaw Petit and Jamsetjee Nusserwanjee Tata accumulated wealth from exports to China and raw cotton shipments to England; Seth Hukumchand and the ancestors of G.D. Birla also traded with China. Other capital came from trade with Burma, the Middle East and East Africa, and from commercial groups operating within India. As colonial control tightened, Indian merchants were barred from trading manufactured goods with Europe, had to export raw materials and food grains, and were edged out of shipping. Till the First World War European Managing Agencies controlled a large sector of Indian industries: Indian financiers provided capital while the agencies made all investment and business decisions.

concepts.label: Where Did the Workers Come From?
concepts.cardText: With the expansion of factories the demand for workers increased: there were 584,000 workers in Indian factories in 1901 and over 2,436,000 by 1946. In most industrial regions workers came from districts around: peasants and artisans who found no work in the village went to industrial centres, and over 50 per cent of workers in Bombay cotton industries in 1911 came from neighbouring Ratnagiri. Most millworkers moved between village and city, returning to their villages for harvests and festivals. Over time workers travelled great distances, such as from the United Provinces to the mills of Bombay and Calcutta. Getting jobs was always difficult because the numbers seeking work always exceeded jobs. Industrialists usually employed a jobber, often an old and trusted worker, who got people from his village, ensured them jobs, helped them settle and gave money in a crisis, and so became a person of authority who demanded money and gifts and controlled workers' lives. Factory workers remained a small proportion of the total industrial workforce.

concepts.label: Managing Agencies, Indian Industrialists and the Swadeshi Shift
concepts.cardText: European Managing Agencies, which dominated industrial production in India, were interested in certain products: they established tea and coffee plantations on land acquired cheaply from the colonial government and invested in mining, indigo and jute, mostly products required for export and not for sale in India. When Indian businessmen began setting up industries in the late nineteenth century, they avoided competing with Manchester goods in the Indian market; since yarn was not an important part of British imports, early Indian cotton mills produced coarse cotton yarn rather than fabric, which was used by Indian handloom weavers or exported to China. By the first decade of the twentieth century, as the swadeshi movement gathered momentum nationalists mobilised people to boycott foreign cloth, industrial groups pressed for tariff protection and concessions, and from 1906 Indian yarn exports to China declined because Chinese and Japanese mills flooded the Chinese market. So industrialists shifted from yarn to cloth, and cotton piece-goods production doubled between 1900 and 1912.

concepts.label: The First World War and Indian Industry
concepts.cardText: Till the First World War industrial growth in India was slow. The war created a dramatically new situation: British mills were busy with war production for the army, so Manchester imports into India declined and Indian mills suddenly had a vast home market to supply. As the war prolonged, Indian factories supplied war needs such as jute bags, cloth for army uniforms, tents, leather boots and saddles. New factories were set up, old ones ran multiple shifts, many new workers were employed and everyone worked longer hours, and industrial production boomed. After the war Manchester could never recapture its old position in the Indian market: unable to modernise and compete with the US, Germany and Japan, the British economy crumbled, cotton production collapsed and exports of cotton cloth fell dramatically, while local industrialists consolidated their position, substituting foreign manufactures and capturing the home market.

concepts.label: Small-Scale Industries Predominate
concepts.cardText: While factory industries grew steadily after the war, large industries formed only a small segment of the economy; about 67 per cent of them in 1911 were in Bengal and Bombay, while elsewhere small-scale production predominated. Only a small proportion of the industrial labour force worked in registered factories: 5 per cent in 1911 and 10 per cent in 1931. The rest worked in small workshops and household units, often in alleys and bylanes, invisible to the passer-by. Handicrafts production even expanded in the twentieth century. Cheap machine-made thread wiped out hand spinning in the nineteenth century, but weavers survived, and handloom cloth production almost trebled between 1900 and 1940. This was partly due to technological change: handicrafts people adopt new technology if it improves production without excessively pushing up costs, so by the second decade of the twentieth century weavers were using the fly shuttle, which increased productivity per worker, sped up production and reduced labour demand; by 1941 over 35 per cent of handlooms had fly shuttles. Weavers of finer cloth survived better because the rich bought it even in famines and mills could not imitate specialised weaves such as Banarasi saris, but weavers who expanded production did not necessarily prosper; their labour was integral to industrialisation.

concepts.label: Advertisements and the Making of Consumer Culture
concepts.cardText: When new products are produced people have to be persuaded to buy them. One way new consumers are created is through advertisements, which make products appear desirable and necessary and try to shape people's minds and create new needs. From the beginning of the industrial age advertisements have helped expand markets and shape a new consumer culture. Manchester industrialists put labels on cloth bundles to make the place of manufacture and the company familiar to the buyer and as a mark of quality. Labels carried images of Indian gods and goddesses as if the association gave divine approval to the goods and made a foreign product seem familiar. By the late nineteenth century manufacturers printed calendars, which unlike newspapers could be used even by people who could not read, and which used gods and figures of emperors and nawabs to suggest quality. When Indian manufacturers advertised, the nationalist message was clear: if you care for the nation, buy products Indians produce, so advertisements became a vehicle of the swadeshi message.
